terms.gloss: mutter, murmur, speak under one’s breath
evidence: Liv. 33.31: clam mussantēs (Lewis & Short; not in Cicero or Caesar)
terms.comment: Varro derives it from the sound mū, the least a mute man can say (L.L. 7.101): rightly, an imitative word. Lewis & Short notes that it is not used by Cicero or Caesar.

evidence: Plaut. Mil. 3.1.149: servī murmurant, of grumbling (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: mutter, make a sound: mostly of the peep one is forbidden to make
evidence: Plaut. Amph. 381: Etiam muttīs? — Jam tacēbō.
Ter. And. 505: nihil jam muttīre audeō
terms.comment: From the sound mū. Etiam muttīs? is “Still muttering?”, that is, “Not another word!”

terms.gloss: keep quiet, say nothing aloud; mutter under one’s breath
evidence: Plaut. Mil. 477: mussitābis: plūs oportet scīre servom quam loquī
terms.comment: The frequentative of mussō; not in Cicero or Caesar (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Nimis crūdum est hoc pōmum. — Quid tū mussās?
phrases.english: This apple is too green. — What are you muttering?
Still muttering? — I’ll be quiet now.

phrases.latin: Ergō, sī sapis, mussitābis: plūs oportet scīre servom quam loquī.
phrases.english: So, if you’re wise, you’ll keep your mouth shut: a slave ought to know more than he says.

sources: Lewis & Short: musso · Lewis & Short: murmuro · Lewis & Short: mutio · Lewis & Short: mussito
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 349.
Vives quoted from the Latinitas loci collection, checked against a single transcription; a modern school dialogue, not a classical source.
